transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Um... hi. I guess I'm here because... I just have a really hard time sitting still. Like, when I'm supposed to be sitting in the radiology suite, or in my classes... I just feel like I'm crawling out of my skin. I tried to just tough it out for a few months, but... I don't know, I always end up pacing, or shifting around, or just finding some excuse to get up and move. So... yeah.
Have you started or changed the dose of any new medications recently, especially any antipsychotic, anti-nausea, or other psychiatric medications?
Um... no. I don't take anything like that. No new meds or... anything. Just no.
When you feel this need to move, is it linked to worrying thoughts or a sense of dread, or does it feel more like just a physical urge to move with your mind otherwise calm?
Um... no, I don't think it's dread. I'm not really worrying about anything when it happens. It's just... physical, I guess. Like my body just has to move. That's about it.
Did you notice this kind of restlessness and need to move as a child or teenager, or is this something that started more recently?

Um... no, it's not a new thing. It's... I guess it's always been like this. My parents actually still bring up my old elementary school conferences. They say the teachers were always telling them how I was... out of my seat all the time. Or calling out, and just rushing ahead before they even finished giving directions. So... yeah. It was happening way before middle school. It's not just something that started with my radiology training.

Besides the restlessness, do you often find it hard to stay focused on tasks, lose track of what you're doing, or forget things like appointments or where you put items—both at work and in daily life?
Um... no. Not really. I mean, I don't think I lose things more than anyone else. And my focus is... fine, I guess. I just have a hard time sitting still. That's all.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others, blurting out answers before a question is finished, or having trouble waiting your turn in line or conversations?

Um... yeah, I guess so. Sometimes at work, if a supervisor is explaining a positioning step or asking me a question... I kind of just jump in with the answer before they're done talking. And then I realize I missed the part that actually mattered. So... yeah. I do that.

Does this same restlessness or impulsivity—like interrupting people or feeling unable to sit still—also show up in other parts of your life, like at home or in social situations, not just at work or school?

Um... yeah, I guess. It's at home, too. Even if I'm doing something I actually like... like editing photos or sketching... I can't really keep it quiet for very long. I just... start tapping, or humming, or talking to whoever's around. Or getting up a bunch. People at home, or in the lab, they... they usually end up telling me to settle down. So... yeah.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a longstanding (childhood-onset, confirmed via parental/teacher reports of being out-of-seat and blurting answers in elementary school) pattern of motor restlessness, difficulty remaining seated, impulsive interrupting/blurting, and excessive fidgeting/movement. Symptoms are pervasive across multiple settings (work/clinical training, home, social/leisure activities) and are not linked to anxious cognitions or worry, ruling out an anxiety disorder. There is no recent medication change (e.g., antipsychotics) to suggest drug-induced akathisia, and the restlessness is purely motoric rather than accompanied by internal dread, further arguing against akathisia. Inattentive symptoms (losing items, poor focus, forgetfulness) were specifically denied, indicating a hyperactive-impulsive predominant presentation rather than combined or inattentive type. The chronicity, early childhood onset, cross-situational impairment, and characteristic hyperactive-impulsive symptom cluster support a diagnosis of Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, hyperactivity-impulsivity predominant presentation (ICD-10 F90.0).
